nim.title: Net interest margin
nim.content:
Net interest margin (NIM) is net interest income divided by average interest-earning assets -- the spread a bank earns between what it pays for deposits/wholesale funding and what it charges on loans.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: NIM has drifted down to 1.89% in H1 FY2026 as mortgage competition and deposit switching to higher-rate savings products compress the spread; a stable or widening NIM is the single biggest lever on bank earnings because it applies to a ~A$1.1tn balance sheet.

What to watch:

  • Sequential half-on-half direction, not the year-on-year level
  • Mortgage front-book vs back-book pricing and deposit mix shifting toward term deposits
  • Whether margin pressure is being offset by volume growth

cet1.title: CET1 capital ratio
cet1.content:
Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio is a bank's highest-quality capital (ordinary equity less deductions) divided by risk-weighted assets -- the primary regulatory solvency measure.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: APRA's "unquestionably strong" benchmark for the major banks is around 10.25%; Westpac has run at 12.2-12.5% through the period shown, well above the floor, which is what funds the ordinary dividend, the FY2024 special dividend and ongoing buybacks.

What to watch:

  • Buffer above the ~10.25% regulatory minimum -- the excess is capital available for buybacks or specials
  • Drawdown from provision top-ups (e.g. the H1 FY2026 Middle-East energy exposure) or RWA growth outpacing capital generation

roeRote.title: Return on equity and return on tangible equity
roeRote.content:
ROE is net income over average shareholders' equity; ROTE uses tangible equity (equity less goodwill and other intangibles) as the denominator, stripping out capital that doesn't generate returns.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: ROTE (~10.6-11.4%) running above ROE (~9.4-10.1%) reflects roughly A$10bn of intangibles on the balance sheet; the DCF's residual-income model is built on tangible book value, so ROTE versus the cost of equity is the direct test of whether the bank is creating or destroying value per dollar of tangible capital.

What to watch:

  • ROTE trend versus the DCF's cost-of-equity assumption (the spread is the value-creation signal)
  • Whether ROE/ROTE improvement comes from margin or from buybacks shrinking the denominator

incomeMix.title: Net interest income vs non-interest income
incomeMix.content:
Net interest income is the spread earned on the lending book; non-interest income is fees, trading and other income not tied to the loan book.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: net interest income is roughly 6x non-interest income, so NIM compression cannot be offset by fee growth the way it can at a more diversified bank -- Westpac's earnings are a leveraged bet on the lending spread.

What to watch:

  • Non-interest income declining as a share of the mix (regulatory and competitive pressure on fees)
  • Trading income volatility distorting a single half

bookValue.title: Book value and tangible book value per share
bookValue.content:
Book value per share is shareholders' equity divided by shares on issue; tangible book value per share (NTA/share) additionally deducts goodwill and other intangibles.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: the DCF values the bank on tangible book value, not book value -- projecting NTA/share forward with retained earnings, capitalising residual income above the cost of equity, and applying an exit price-to-tangible-book multiple. The ~A$3/share gap between the two lines is goodwill and other intangibles that residual-income investors exclude.

What to watch:

  • NTA/share growth rate versus the dividend payout (retained earnings compound NTA)
  • The market price-to-tangible-book multiple versus the DCF's exit multiple assumption

payoutRatio.title: Dividend payout ratio
payoutRatio.content:
Dividend payout ratio is ordinary dividends paid divided by net income -- how much of earnings is distributed versus retained to build capital.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: the payout ratio has run 69-78% across the period. FY2024 also included a 15 cent special dividend (on top of the regular per-share dividend shown elsewhere on this page) funded from surplus capital after the CommIS sale and the buffer above APRA's CET1 minimum -- it is not included in this ratio, which would otherwise look like an isolated payout spike that year.

What to watch:

  • A rising payout ratio that isn't matched by CET1 headroom
  • Special dividends/buybacks as the release valve for excess capital rather than higher regular DPS

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Westpac Banking Corporation: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Westpac Banking Corporation: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
